modalities.name: No Rehearsal Outing
modalities.tagline: Doing the errand you keep rehearsing, with a coach beside you.
modalities.whatItIs: No Rehearsal Outing is a new, untested concept that takes acceptance-based skills out of the therapy room and into one real task you have been rehearsing in your head, such as returning an item or asking a question at a counter. A coach or trained peer goes with you, but there is no preparation, script or talk about the past. The only material is what happens in front of you, met as it comes.
modalities.coreIdea: Mental rehearsal and replay can feel like preparation while keeping you out of the actual moment, so the practice is to do the real thing with no rehearsal at all and meet it with open senses.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick an everyday task you have been putting off and rehearsing, and meet the coach on the spot, for example outside the shop, without planning what to say. While you do it, the coach stays nearby and, if you freeze, quietly asks what you can see and hear right now; afterwards you spend ten minutes together noting what actually happened compared with what your rehearsals predicted. Over four outings the tasks get a little harder.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rehearse conversations and errands for days beforehand and replay them afterwards, and who want to practice meeting real moments as they come, with someone alongside.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care: if rehearsing and avoiding are driven by severe social anxiety, panic or trauma, work with a qualified clinician first. Tasks are chosen together and kept safe and legal, and you can stop an outing at any time.
modalities.tweet: New concept: the No Rehearsal Outing. You do the errand you've been rehearsing for days (returning something, asking at a counter) with a coach nearby and no script, then compare what happened with what your head predicted. For chronic rehearsers.

modalities.name: Events, Not Characters
modalities.tagline: Thoughts and urges described as plain passing events, not inner people.
modalities.whatItIs: Events, Not Characters is a proposed peer practice that pushes acceptance work in the opposite direction from approaches that give the mind a cast of inner parts. Nothing inside you is treated as a person with a history or a motive: a worry is just 'a thought about money, now', and an urge is just 'a pull toward the phone, now'. It stays in the present, leans on what you can actually notice, and needs no therapist once learned.
modalities.coreIdea: Describing inner experience as plain, present events rather than as characters with stories is meant to make it easier to watch it pass and still choose what to do.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two people meet for 20 minutes, in person or by video. Each takes five minutes to describe aloud whatever is showing up, using only the form 'there is...' (there is tightness in my chest, there is a thought that I will fail, there is the sound of traffic), while the other listens without comment. Then each names one small action they will take that day, whether or not the thoughts come along.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get tangled in long inner arguments and stories about themselves, and who want a light, present-focused habit they can share with a friend.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea, not therapy: plain describing can still bring up strong feelings or memories, and anyone with trauma, dissociation or a mental health crisis should work with a qualified clinician instead. Partners agree to keep what is said private and to stop whenever either wants.
modalities.tweet: An idea for two friends and 20 minutes: take turns describing what's going on inside using only 'there is...' (there is tension, there is a worried thought). No inner characters, no backstory. Just events passing, then one small step you care about.

modalities.name: Unscored Weeks
modalities.tagline: Stop rating your feelings for a while, and simply let them be.
modalities.whatItIs: Unscored Weeks is a new, untested concept for people who constantly measure their inner life: rating anxiety out of ten, checking whether a feeling has gone, tracking every mood. It takes acceptance much further than usual and loosens structure almost completely, with no worksheets, no goals and no progress charts. A teacher or a short written guide explains the idea, and after that the practice is yours.
modalities.coreIdea: Constantly scoring and checking feelings can keep attention locked on them, so for a set period you stop measuring and give every feeling permission to be exactly as strong as it is.
modalities.whatYouDo: For two weeks you hand your mood apps and symptom ratings to a teacher, or simply switch them off, and agree not to rate, log or check how you feel. Instead, at the end of each day you name one thing you did that mattered to you, with no number attached. You meet the teacher once a week to talk about how life feels without the scores, not about whether feelings went down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel worn out by monitoring their own minds, for example by checking again and again whether worry or sadness has lifted, and who want to try living alongside feelings without keeping score.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a replacement for care: do not stop any tracking a doctor or therapist has asked for, such as a mood or medication diary, and get professional help promptly if low mood, anxiety or thoughts of self-harm grow worse. Letting feelings be is not the same as putting up with harmful situations.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Unscored Weeks. Exhausted by monitoring your own mind? For two weeks you stop rating your moods, checking whether the anxiety is gone or tracking progress, and let feelings be as big as they are.

modalities.name: Leave the Why Alone
modalities.tagline: Sessions with one rule: no asking why, only what now.
modalities.whatItIs: Leave the Why Alone is a proposed calm, one-to-one practice for living with a feeling that keeps coming back, such as a familiar dread or irritability, without searching for the hidden reason behind it. A practitioner holds a single rule for the conversation: whenever a 'why' question starts, it is set aside in favor of 'what is here now?' and 'what matters next?'. Nothing about the past is explored, and the tone stays quiet and settling.
modalities.coreIdea: A feeling can be allowed, noticed in the present and carried into a meaningful day without first being understood, and dropping the search for 'why' may itself bring some ease.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over four calm 40-minute sessions, you describe the recurring feeling as it is now, where it sits in the body and what it pulls you to do. Each time you start explaining its cause, the practitioner gently names it ('that's a why') and asks what you notice right now instead, then helps you choose one thing that matters this week with the feeling along for the ride. Between sessions you try the same rule on your own when the feeling arrives.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have spent a long time analyzing a recurring feeling and are tired of the search, and who want a gentle way to get on with life while it is there.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea, not a replacement for medical or psychological care: a new or changing feeling, or persistent low mood or anxiety, should be checked by a doctor or therapist, since some causes need medical attention. Leaving the why alone means not ruminating, not ignoring warning signs or harmful situations.
modalities.tweet: Worn out by analyzing the same feeling for years? Imagine a session with one rule: no asking why. A gentle new idea: a practitioner steers you from explaining the feeling to what's here now and what matters next.

modalities.name: The Metaphor Kitchen
modalities.tagline: A small group cooks up metaphors that loosen each other's stuck stories.
modalities.whatItIs: The Metaphor Kitchen is a new, untested group format that works entirely through words and imagination, the far opposite of body-based practices that need no talking at all. Acceptance-based therapy already leans on metaphors, such as struggling in quicksand; here, inventing fresh metaphors together is the whole session. A trained facilitator guides a group of five to eight people.
modalities.coreIdea: Turning a stuck problem into a vivid image, such as a tug of war or a radio that never switches off, is meant to give a little distance from it and suggest a different way to respond.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 90-minute session, one person describes a struggle in a few sentences and the group spends ten minutes offering metaphors for it, which the facilitator writes on a board. The person picks the one that feels most true and the group explores it: what happens if you drop the rope, or let the radio play while you cook? Everyone leaves with one image to recall during the week and one step they will take with it in mind.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think in pictures and stories, who find body-based or silent practices hard to connect with, and who enjoy the creativity and company of a group.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: a metaphor offered by someone else can feel dismissive or hurtful, so the facilitator keeps everything voluntary and the person can reject every suggestion. People in crisis or with severe depression, trauma or psychosis should get individual care from a qualified clinician rather than rely on a group.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: a 'metaphor kitchen'. A small group hears your stuck problem and cooks up images for it (a tug of war, a radio that won't switch off), you pick the one that fits, and then you try dropping the rope.

modalities.name: The Values Wordsmith
modalities.tagline: A coach helps you sharpen what you stand for into one sentence.
modalities.whatItIs: The Values Wordsmith is a proposed coaching format that moves acceptance-based work away from slow, body-felt exploration and toward precise language and action. Instead of waiting for a vague bodily sense to suggest words, you and a coach deliberately draft, test and rewrite a statement of what you care about. It is brisk, word-based and change-oriented, and it stays in the present.
modalities.coreIdea: A value put into exact, personal words is easier to act on, so the work is to turn a vague sense of what matters into a sentence sharp enough to guide a real choice this week.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over three or four 45-minute sessions, you bring a life area, such as work or friendship, and the coach asks pointed questions while you write and rewrite a single sentence about how you want to show up there. Each week you test the sentence on one real decision and report back where it helped, where it was vague, and which thoughts tried to talk you out of acting on it. You keep the final sentences together on one card.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like clear language and concrete plans, who feel vague about what they want, and who find inward, body-focused practices too slow or hard to read.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea and coaching rather than therapy: values work can surface grief or guilt about how life has gone, and anyone with severe depression or suicidal thoughts should see a qualified clinician first. Values are meant as a compass, not a new set of rules to fail at.
modalities.tweet: New idea: The Values Wordsmith. A coach helps you rewrite what you care about until it's one sharp sentence, then you test it on a real decision each week. Plain words instead of slow inner work, and a compass, not a rulebook.

modalities.name: Set by a Friend
modalities.tagline: A friend picks your small daily step toward what matters.
modalities.whatItIs: Set by a Friend is a new, untested routine that turns psychological flexibility into small daily steps, moving away from open, presence-based coaching toward structure and action. Two friends who know what the other cares about choose one small, value-linked step for each other every evening, so each of you gets steps you might not have picked yourself, while keeping the right to say no. A coach helps you set it up and checks in weekly.
modalities.coreIdea: Flexibility may grow through many small chances to act on what matters while uncomfortable thoughts come along, and having a friend choose the step is meant to stop you steering around the ones your mind most wants to avoid.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start you each write down three things you care about, the kinds of step you are willing to be set and any areas that are off limits. Each evening you text your friend one small step for the next day, such as 'say one honest thing in the team meeting, even if your mind calls it pointless', and the following evening you each reply with one line on what happened and which thoughts showed up, without scoring. Once a week the coach joins a ten-minute call to resize steps that were too big or too small and to check that both of you still feel free to say no.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them but tend to choose only the comfortable version, and who keep a habit going better with a friend than alone.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and a self-help habit, not a substitute for care: you can always swap or refuse a step, and a friend never sets anything unsafe, costly, illegal or involving other people's private lives. People with severe depression, trauma or a crisis should work with a qualified clinician, and if the routine starts to strain the friendship, pause it and talk.
modalities.tweet: Prototype routine: Set by a Friend. Each evening a friend who knows your values texts you one small step for tomorrow (say the honest thing in the meeting), you do it with whatever thoughts tag along, then trade one line. You can always say no.

modalities.name: Public Promise Circle
modalities.tagline: Say one valued step out loud, then report back honestly next week.
modalities.whatItIs: Public Promise Circle is a proposed facilitated group that pushes the commitment side of acceptance-based therapy as far as it will go, the opposite of practices that drop all intention and control. A trained facilitator runs a fixed weekly protocol for six to eight people, centered on stating a value-based action in front of others and reporting back. It does not argue with thoughts: they are simply brought along while you act.
modalities.coreIdea: Making a small commitment in public, and later saying honestly what happened, including the thoughts and feelings that got in the way, is meant to turn values into action without needing to feel ready first.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 75-minute session follows the same steps: a short present-moment exercise, a round in which everyone reports on last week's promise without being judged, a round in which each person states one specific step for the coming week and the value behind it, and a closing minute of silence. The facilitator helps people shrink promises that are too big and notice the 'reasons' their minds offer for not following through. The group runs for eight weeks with the same members.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them but keep putting it off, and who are motivated by structure, company and a gentle sense of accountability.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: public promises can feed shame or perfectionism if handled harshly, so the facilitator keeps the tone kind and welcomes a missed step as information, not failure. People with social anxiety, severe depression or a current crisis should talk to a clinician first and can join at their own pace.
modalities.tweet: A proposal: the Public Promise Circle. Each week you tell a small group one step you'll take toward what matters, then come back and say honestly what happened, excuses included. Kind accountability for people who keep putting their own life on hold.

modalities.name: Other Eyes Interviews
modalities.tagline: A guide interviews you from other people's points of view.
modalities.whatItIs: Other Eyes Interviews is a proposed one-to-one practice that seeks insight through conversation and imagination rather than through silent watching of body sensations. It builds on the idea in acceptance-based therapy that you are more than your point of view, and makes perspective-taking the main activity: a trained guide interviews you as if you were other people looking at your situation. Between sessions you gather real views from friends.
modalities.coreIdea: Speaking about your problem as your future self, a kind friend or a curious child would, and hearing how real friends see it, is meant to loosen the grip of the one view that feels like the only truth.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a lively 50-minute session, the guide asks you to describe a current problem in your own voice, then interviews you in turn as yourself ten years from now, as a friend who loves you and as a curious child, asking each what they see that you are missing. Before the next session you ask two real friends one question, how they see it, and bring their answers back to compare. You finish each session by naming one step that now seems possible.
modalities.whoItsFor: Talkative, imaginative people who find silent meditation dull or lonely, and anyone stuck in one rigid view of a situation.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea: talking through a painful problem from other angles can stir strong feelings, and friends' views can hurt, so you choose whom to ask and the guide keeps it to present-day concerns. People with severe depression, trauma or a crisis should get help from a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Speculative practice: Other Eyes Interviews. A guide interviews you about your problem as your future self, a friend who loves you and a curious kid would see it, then you ask two real friends how they see it. For chatty people stuck in one view.

modalities.name: No Audience Needed
modalities.tagline: Quiet, valued actions done with no audience, score or praise.
modalities.whatItIs: No Audience Needed is a new, untested concept that pushes acceptance-based work as far as possible from high-intensity, measured, performance-driven effort. In calm one-to-one conversations, a trained practitioner guides you toward small actions that matter to you and that no one will ever see, count or praise. The practice is making room for the restless urge to be noticed while the deed stays quiet.
modalities.coreIdea: When effort is always aimed at results or applause, values can get lost behind performance, so doing what matters with no audience at all is meant to let you feel why it matters for its own sake.
modalities.whatYouDo: In slow, relaxed weekly sessions you and the practitioner pick a value, such as kindness or care for your surroundings, and choose a few unseen acts for the week, like leaving an anonymous kind note or tidying a shared space before anyone arrives. You tell no one and post nothing, and when the itch to mention it comes, you notice it and let it pass. In the next session you talk about what doing it unseen felt like, without rating how well it went.
modalities.whoItsFor: High achievers and people who feel their worth depends on being seen, praised or ahead, and who want a calmer, quieter relationship with what they care about.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care: if the drive to achieve comes with exhaustion, low mood or thoughts of self-harm, see a qualified clinician. Unseen acts are always small, safe and legal, and never mean hiding from people who need to know what you are doing.
modalities.tweet: Does your worth ride on being seen? Concept sketch: No Audience Needed. With a calm guide, you pick small acts that matter (an anonymous kind note, tidying before anyone arrives), tell no one, and let the urge to be noticed pass.

modalities.name: Without the Jersey
modalities.tagline: Alone, imagining a day with every role taken away.
modalities.whatItIs: Without the Jersey is a new, untested solitary practice that turns away from team play, physical effort and social roles toward stillness, imagination and time alone. Guided by a script your therapist writes for you, you picture an ordinary day in which every role you hold has been taken away: no job title, team, family label or reputation. What you would still want to do in that day points to values that do not depend on any role.
modalities.coreIdea: When worth rides on a role, losing it can feel like losing yourself, so imagining life with no roles at all is meant to show what you care about underneath them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone in a quiet room, you listen to a 20-minute recording in which your therapist slowly walks you through a day from waking to sleep, with no one expecting anything of you because of who you are. At each scene you note what you would still choose to do, whom you would still want to see and what you would miss. Every two weeks you meet the therapist to turn those notes into small steps that do not rely on any one role.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose sense of worth rides on one role, such as athletes after an injury, people between jobs, new retirees or parents whose children have left home.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: imagining life without your roles can stir grief or emptiness, so you can stop the recording at any time and the therapist checks in regularly. People with severe depression, a recent loss or a crisis should work with a qualified clinician in person rather than alone with recordings.
modalities.tweet: New practice idea for anyone whose worth rides on a role (athlete, boss, parent): Without the Jersey. Alone, you follow a recording that walks you through a day with every role taken away, and notice what you'd still care about.

modalities.name: Permission to Stop
modalities.tagline: Learning when pushing on serves your values, and when it doesn't.
modalities.whatItIs: Permission to Stop is a new, untested concept for people who live as if life were an endurance event, always pushing through tiredness, pain or doubt on their own. It moves acceptance-based work away from self-propelled effort toward stillness, calm and close guidance from a trained practitioner. Its focus is flexible persistence: knowing when to keep going for what matters and when stopping is the braver, more honest choice.
modalities.coreIdea: Persistence is only useful when it serves your values, so the practice is to notice the difference between steady commitment and rigid, exhausting pushing that is really a way of avoiding something.
modalities.whatYouDo: In six weekly, seated, 50-minute sessions, you and the practitioner look at one area where you always push on, such as work or training, and map when persistence has helped and when it has cost you sleep, health or relationships. You practice noticing the thoughts that say 'stopping means failing', making room for the guilt that comes with resting, and choosing one planned stop each week. You then review together what happened when you stopped.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are proud of their grit but are running on empty, including overworkers, carers and athletes who struggle to rest or ask for help.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a replacement for medical care: ongoing exhaustion can have physical causes and is worth checking with a doctor, and burnout with low mood or thoughts of self-harm calls for professional help. Stopping here means planned rest in line with your values, not dropping important responsibilities without support.
modalities.tweet: New practice idea: Permission to Stop. With a guide, you sort out when pushing on serves what you care about and when it's just exhausting habit, then practice one planned stop a week, guilt and all. Grit and fuel are not the same thing.

modalities.name: Living Inside the Limit
modalities.tagline: Making peace with a real limit, and living fully inside it.
modalities.whatItIs: Living Inside the Limit is a proposed guided practice that turns away from the logic of getting ever stronger and instead makes acceptance of real limits the center of the work. Some limits, such as a long-term illness, aging, caring duties or a disability, cannot simply be trained away. With a trained practitioner and a loose, conversational format, you practice letting the limit be there and finding what still matters inside it.
modalities.coreIdea: Struggling against a limit that cannot change can use up the energy you need for living, so the practice is to stop fighting the limit itself and ask what a meaningful life looks like within it.
modalities.whatYouDo: In relaxed weekly conversations, you name a limit you keep fighting and notice the thoughts and grief it brings, without trying to argue them away. The practitioner helps you list what you value and find small ways to live those values within the limit, for example staying close to friends by phone on low-energy days. There are no targets or progress charts, only a weekly look at what felt more livable.
modalities.whoItsFor: People living with a lasting limit, such as chronic illness, pain, disability or age-related change, who are tired of measuring themselves against what they used to be able to do.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea meant to sit alongside medical care, never to replace it: keep up any prescribed care, and do not accept a limit as permanent until a doctor has assessed it. Grief about lost abilities can be heavy, and persistent low mood deserves professional help.
modalities.tweet: A new concept for anyone living with a limit that won't train away (illness, pain, age): Living Inside the Limit. With a guide you stop fighting the limit itself and look for what still matters inside it. No targets, no progress charts.

modalities.name: Creature Sketchbook
modalities.tagline: Draw your recurring feelings as imagined creatures, then walk on together.
modalities.whatItIs: Creature Sketchbook is a new, untested practice that swaps the real, calming animal of animal-assisted work for imagined creatures you invent yourself. Each recurring feeling or thought, such as worry or self-criticism, gets drawn or described as a creature with a size, color and habits. You learn it with a practitioner, who looks through the sketchbook with you now and then, and you practice letting each creature come along while you do what matters.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving a feeling a playful, concrete form is meant to create a little distance from it, making it easier to notice when it shows up and to act on your values anyway.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a first session the practitioner helps you sketch the creature that shows up most and agree on its name. Then once a week you spend 15 minutes drawing or describing the creature that showed up most, what set it off and what it told you to do, and on the opposite page one thing you did anyway; when it appears during the day, you greet it silently by name ('hello, Grumble') and carry on. Every month you and the practitioner look through the pages together.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like drawing, doodling or playful writing, and who want a light way to relate differently to familiar worries, with occasional support.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, not a substitute for care: if drawing a feeling makes it feel bigger or more frightening, stop and tell your practitioner. People with severe anxiety, depression, trauma or psychosis should work with a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Invented practice: the Creature Sketchbook. Draw your recurring worry as a creature (size, color, habits), give it a name, and when it shows up say hello and keep doing what matters. A playful way to stop wrestling with the same old feeling 🐉

modalities.name: Mind Play-by-Play
modalities.tagline: Commentating aloud on your mind's moves during an ordinary task.
modalities.whatItIs: Mind Play-by-Play is a proposed coached practice that moves acceptance-based work away from calm, slow, body-centered forms toward lively work with the mind in the middle of action. While you do an ordinary, low-stakes task in session, such as sorting papers or planning a meal, you describe aloud what your mind is doing, the way a sports commentator describes a match. A trained coach sits beside you, one to one, and keeps the commentary going.
modalities.coreIdea: Calling the mind's tactics as they happen, such as 'and here comes its favorite move, telling me it's too late', is meant to keep you a step back from them, so you can keep doing what matters while they play out.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session you pick an everyday task and, for 20 minutes, speak a running third-person commentary on your mind as you work: what it says, what it tries and how loud it gets, such as 'and now it's comparing me to my sister again'. The coach prompts you to keep commenting and keep working, without arguing with any thought. Afterwards you note your mind's three favorite moves and try ten minutes of silent commentary on your own each day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds keep up a constant running argument, and who like a lively, slightly playful way to watch it instead of being swept along.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: speaking your thoughts aloud can feel exposing, so the coach keeps the tone respectful and you can stop at any point. It is not suited to times of crisis, severe depression or thoughts of self-harm, which need a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Experimental idea: Mind Play-by-Play. While you sort papers or plan dinner, you commentate on your own mind like a sports match ('and now it's comparing me to my sister again') with a coach keeping you going. Watch the game instead of being the ball.

modalities.name: Alone on Purpose
modalities.tagline: Timed, planned solitude for people who find being alone unbearable.
modalities.whatItIs: Alone on Purpose is a new, untested concept that pushes acceptance-based work away from company and toward structured solitude. Under a therapist's plan, you spend set periods alone without phone, screens or other distractions, practicing making room for whatever shows up, such as boredom, loneliness or restlessness. The therapist designs each step and reviews it with you, but the practice itself is done on your own.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people fill every gap with noise or company to avoid uncomfortable feelings, so learning to be with yourself in short, planned doses is meant to make solitude less frightening and your choices freer.
modalities.whatYouDo: Week by week the therapist sets a solitude period, starting at ten minutes and building toward an hour, which you spend sitting, walking indoors or doing a simple task with no devices. Each time, you note on a short form which urges and feelings came up and how you made room for them. In a weekly session you go through the forms together and plan the next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot bear a quiet moment without reaching for a phone or company, and who want to feel less driven by boredom or loneliness.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: for someone who is already isolated or lonely, more time alone may not help, so the therapist checks that solitude is a choice and keeps real-world connection in the plan. Stop and get support if low mood or distressing thoughts grow stronger when you are alone.
modalities.tweet: Could being alone be a skill you train in small doses? An untested idea: Alone on Purpose. Ten device-free minutes alone, then more, making room for boredom and loneliness as they show up, with a therapist planning each step.

modalities.name: The Imagined First Step
modalities.tagline: Rehearsing a scary, valued step in imagination, with the fear allowed.
modalities.whatItIs: The Imagined First Step is a proposed indoor, therapist-led practice that moves acceptance-based work away from open-air, unplanned, sense-based experience toward structured imagination. You vividly picture yourself taking a step you care about but fear, such as speaking up at a meeting, while practicing letting the fear be there. The aim is not to make the fear go down but to rehearse carrying it while you act.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagining a valued step in rich detail, with the feelings it brings allowed rather than fought, is meant to build willingness before you try the step in real life.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a set 50-minute session, the therapist helps you pick one valued step and break it into scenes, then guides you through each scene with your eyes closed while you describe what you see and feel. Whenever fear or a 'you can't' thought shows up, you pause, name it, make room for it and continue the scene. You finish by agreeing on a real-world version of the step for the coming week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what they want to do but freeze when the moment comes, and who find it helpful to practice in their heads before acting.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea: imagined scenes can bring strong anxiety, so the therapist moves at your pace and you can open your eyes at any time. It is not meant for trauma memories, which call for a clinician trained in trauma care.
modalities.tweet: Novel concept: The Imagined First Step. With a therapist, you vividly imagine the scary step you care about (speaking up, asking someone out) and let the fear come along instead of fighting it. Then you take the step for real.

modalities.name: Admired Moments Exchange
modalities.tagline: Finding your values in the moments you admire in others.
modalities.whatItIs: Admired Moments Exchange is a new, untested group format that moves acceptance-based values work away from plain sensory contact with the present and into shared memory and imagination. Instead of asking what you value directly, each member brings a vivid story of a moment when someone they admire acted in a way that moved them. The group listens for the value inside each story, and a trained facilitator keeps the focus on qualities, not achievements.
modalities.coreIdea: What we admire in others often points to what we want for ourselves, so collecting admired moments is meant to reveal values that are hard to name head-on.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to ten people meet for two hours, and each tells a two-minute story of an admired moment, such as a grandparent apologizing to a child or a colleague speaking up for someone. Others call out the qualities they heard and the facilitator writes them on a shared wall, so by the end the group has a large map of values in plain words. Each person then picks one quality from the wall and one admired person to quietly imitate in a small way for a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who go blank when asked what they value, who feel they are drifting, and who are energized by stories and company.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: stories about admired people can stir grief, envy or self-criticism, so telling one is optional, it comes only from moments you already remember and is never a search for forgotten ones, and the images and feelings it brings are not evidence of exactly what happened. The facilitator leaves time to talk afterwards, and people who are grieving, severely depressed or in crisis should talk to a qualified clinician first.
modalities.tweet: Picture someone you admire doing the thing that moved you. A new group idea: everyone tells one such moment, the group names the qualities inside it, and each person picks one to quietly imitate for a week. Telling one is always optional.

modalities.name: Before You Press Play
modalities.tagline: Making room for a feeling before reaching for music to change it.
modalities.whatItIs: Before You Press Play is a new, untested concept that takes acceptance-based work away from using music, podcasts or noise to manage mood. It looks at the moments when you reach for headphones to drown out or lift a feeling, and asks you to pause first and let the feeling be there for a minute. A practitioner guides the practice in a few calm one-to-one sessions, and music stays welcome afterwards.
modalities.coreIdea: Using sound to switch feelings off can quietly become a way of never meeting them, so a short, willing pause before pressing play is meant to make music a choice rather than an escape.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a first session you and the practitioner map when you reach for sound, such as on the commute, while falling asleep or after a hard call, and which feelings those moments hold. For two weeks, whenever you go to press play, you first spend one quiet minute noticing the feeling, naming it and letting it stay, then choose whether to play something at all. Weekly sessions look at what you noticed, without judging how often you chose music.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who can't sit with a feeling without headphones in, and who want sound to be a pleasure rather than a way of never feeling anything.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, not a substitute for care: if music is how you get through severe distress, panic or thoughts of self-harm, keep using it and see a qualified clinician first. The pause is always optional, and music is never something to give up for good.
modalities.tweet: Before you reach for headphones to drown out a feeling, what if you gave it one quiet minute first? A new idea: Before You Press Play. A practitioner helps you map those moments, so music becomes a choice, not an escape.

modalities.name: Live Surprise Sessions
modalities.tagline: The old fear meets a live, real-time surprise, right in the session.
modalities.whatItIs: Live Surprise Sessions is a new, untested concept that takes the idea of unlocking an old emotional learning and looks for the contradiction in real, present experience rather than in imagined scenes or soothing imagery. A trained therapist helps you find the hidden rule behind a symptom, such as 'if I say no, people leave', and then sets up a small, live moment in the session that breaks it. It is emotionally charged and stays closer to recent life than to early childhood.
modalities.coreIdea: An old emotional prediction may loosen most when it is fully active and something real happens right now that it did not predict, so the session itself becomes the place where the surprise happens.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over several weekly sessions, the therapist helps you put the hidden rule into words and feel how true it seems. Then, with your agreement, you test it live: for example, you say a clear 'no' to the therapist, or show irritation, and you both notice what actually happens, for instance that the relationship holds. Later sessions check whether similar situations outside still set off the old reaction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already understand where a pattern comes from but still feel it in their bones, and who want to experience, not just discuss, something that contradicts it.
modalities.cautions: This untested idea is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, and although the work is mostly about the present, any memories it touches are ones you already have, which are not evidence of what happened and are never used to uncover forgotten events. Every live test is agreed in advance, never deceptive or unsafe, and stopped if your distress climbs, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis need stabilization first.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Live Surprise Sessions. A trauma-trained therapist helps you name the old rule behind a pattern ('if I say no, people leave'), then you test it live: you say no, and you both see what really happens. Knowing why isn't feeling it.

modalities.name: The Slowed Moment
modalities.tagline: One three-second trigger, replayed slowly until its hidden prediction shows.
modalities.whatItIs: The Slowed Moment is a proposed structured method that pushes the emotional-learning approach toward precision and change, and away from approaches that work through a cast of inner parts. Instead of mapping a whole inner family, a trained therapist and client take one recent moment when a symptom fired, such as a flash of panic in a meeting, and slow it down frame by frame. The goal is to catch the exact emotional prediction that made the reaction feel necessary.
modalities.coreIdea: A strong reaction contains a fast, hidden forecast of what would happen otherwise, and slowing a single trigger moment right down is meant to bring that forecast into words so it can be checked against what you now know.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute session, you replay a recent trigger in your mind as if in slow motion, and the therapist stops you at each instant to ask what you saw, felt and expected would happen next. When the forecast surfaces, for example 'they will see I'm a fraud and I'll be thrown out', you say it aloud and feel how true it seems. The therapist then helps you bring in what you also know to be true, and later sessions check the same kind of moment again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a reaction that hits too fast to understand, such as sudden panic, rage or shutting down, who want a precise, step-by-step way to see what drives it.
modalities.cautions: Untested so far, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care and works only from recent moments you already remember: images and feelings that surface while replaying are not evidence of what happened, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. Replaying a trigger can bring strong emotion, so the pace stays in your control, and it should not replace well-tested treatments for panic or PTSD without professional advice.
modalities.tweet: For reactions that hit too fast to understand, a new idea: The Slowed Moment. With a therapist you replay one 3-second trigger frame by frame until the hidden forecast shows ('they'll see I'm a fraud'), then check it against what you know now.

modalities.name: Where It Began
modalities.tagline: An open, unhurried search for where a reaction first made sense.
modalities.whatItIs: Where It Began is a new, untested concept that pushes emotional-learning work deeper into the past and further from structured, present-focused methods. There is no agenda, worksheet or set number of sessions: a highly trained therapist follows the client slowly back toward the earliest remembered experiences in which a symptom made emotional sense. Nothing is pushed to change; the original learning is first felt and understood at your own pace.
modalities.coreIdea: A pattern that began as a sensible response to an early situation may only reveal its logic when explored slowly and without pressure, with contradicting knowledge allowed to arise on its own rather than being engineered.
modalities.whatYouDo: In open-ended weekly sessions, you start from a present symptom, such as freezing when criticized, and explore with the therapist when you remember feeling this way before, staying with what you already recall rather than searching for anything new. When a remembered situation clearly fits, you put into words what you learned there about yourself and others, at your own pace. The therapist does not hurry toward change, and returns to steadying, present-day topics whenever it gets too much.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to understand a long-standing pattern at its roots, who have found skill-based approaches too fast or structured, and who have the time and support for longer, deeper work.
modalities.cautions: Because this untested idea reaches far back, it is led only by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, who stays with memories you already have, never suggests events and never uses the work to uncover forgotten ones, since images and feelings that arise are not evidence of what happened. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis need stabilization first, and the therapist returns to the present whenever the work gets too much.
modalities.tweet: Speculative concept: Where It Began. No agenda, no worksheets: a trauma-trained therapist helps you slowly connect a present pattern to situations you already remember, letting them be felt before anything changes. Not for digging up forgotten events.

modalities.name: Symptom Across the Years
modalities.tagline: Charting a symptom's whole life story to see what switches it on.
modalities.whatItIs: Symptom Across the Years is a new, untested concept that goes the opposite way from learning to live alongside a symptom: it asks what the symptom has been responding to across your whole life. With a specialist therapist, you build a structured timeline showing when the symptom appeared, when it was strongest and, just as important, when it faded or vanished. Comparing those periods points to the emotional learning that switches it on.
modalities.coreIdea: If a symptom is driven by an old emotional learning, it should rise and fall with the situations that learning reads as dangerous, so the gaps in the timeline are as revealing as the peaks.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over several structured sessions you mark on a long paper timeline the years and situations when the symptom, such as constant worry, was loud, quiet or absent, using only what you already remember. For each loud and quiet period the therapist asks what was different about who was around, what was expected of you and what felt at risk. The contrast is meant to suggest a sentence, such as 'when I'm responsible for others, I must stay on guard', which you then feel and set against contradicting experience.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have had a symptom on and off for years, who like seeing patterns laid out, and who are curious why it comes and goes.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care: the timeline is built only from memories you already have, gaps are never filled in by searching for forgotten events, and nothing on it, including the images and feelings it stirs, counts as evidence of what happened. Looking back across hard years can stir strong feelings, medical causes of a symptom should be ruled out first, and it should not replace well-tested treatments without professional advice.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment you could do with a therapist: chart your symptom across your whole life, including the stretches when it vanished. What was different then? A new concept for people whose symptom comes and goes and who want to know why.

modalities.name: The Witnessed Telling
modalities.tagline: Putting a symptom's hidden logic into words, with a small group listening.
modalities.whatItIs: The Witnessed Telling is a new, untested group format that takes emotional-learning work as far as possible from wordless, body-based practices: everything happens through words, memory and imagination, in front of witnesses. In a small closed group led by a specialist therapist, one member at a time explores why a symptom makes emotional sense and says it aloud. The others listen and, afterwards, say simply what they understood.
modalities.coreIdea: Saying the hidden emotional truth behind a symptom out loud, and seeing other people understand it without judgment, is meant to make it fully conscious and to offer a vivid contrast with the old expectation of being shamed or dismissed.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six people meet weekly for two hours, with a lead therapist and a co-therapist. In each session one or two members work with the therapist for 30 minutes, tracing a symptom back to the emotional learning that drives it and finding the words for it, such as 'if I slip up in front of people, I'll be laughed at'. The group then reflects back what they heard, and everyone closes by naming one thing they recognized in themselves.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry shame about a symptom or pattern, who feel very alone with it, and who want both depth and the experience of being understood by others.
modalities.cautions: The group is an untested idea led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care with a co-therapist, and members speak only from memories they already have: what comes up is not evidence of what happened, and the group is never used to uncover forgotten events. Careful screening comes first, members agree to confidentiality and choose how much to share, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should start with individual care.
modalities.tweet: Untested group idea: The Witnessed Telling. One person at a time works with a trauma-trained therapist to put into words why their symptom makes sense ('if I slip up in front of people, I'll be laughed at'), while a few others just listen, without judging.

modalities.name: Who Is It For?
modalities.tagline: Finding the person a symptom is silently speaking to.
modalities.whatItIs: Who Is It For? is a new, untested concept that moves emotional-learning work away from slow, quiet waiting for a bodily felt sense and toward a sharp, emotionally charged question about relationships. It starts from the idea that some patterns, such as holding back at work or picking the same fight, may carry a message to a particular person that sits outside awareness; symptoms are never chosen or faked, and any message is only one strand among their many causes. A specialist therapist helps you find that person and what the pattern seems to be saying to them.
modalities.coreIdea: If a pattern is partly an unspoken message, it may feel less necessary once the message, and the person it is meant for, are known and it can be expressed or answered in another way.
modalities.whatYouDo: You describe the last time the pattern showed up, and the therapist asks you to imagine who would most need to see it, then to picture that person watching and notice what you feel and what you want them to understand. When a message comes into words, such as 'see how much you hurt me' or 'don't leave me alone', you say it aloud and feel its weight. Later sessions look for other, safer ways that message could be said or answered, and check whether the pattern still feels needed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose recurring pattern seems tied up with a particular relationship, and who are curious what it might be trying to say.
modalities.cautions: This untested idea is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, works only with memories and relationships you already know, and is never used to uncover forgotten events; the person who comes to mind, and any image or feeling about them, is not evidence of what they did or of what happened. Finding a message is about understanding, never blaming or confronting anyone, and medical causes of any symptom must be ruled out first.
modalities.tweet: Idea: some patterns may quietly speak to someone ('see how much you hurt me', 'don't leave me'). With a trauma-trained therapist, you ask who yours is for and what it's saying, then look for safer ways to say it. No blame, no confrontation.

modalities.name: Symptom Logic Map
modalities.tagline: Drawing the step-by-step chain that makes a symptom feel necessary.
modalities.whatItIs: Symptom Logic Map is a new, untested concept that pushes emotional-learning work toward structure and deliberate change, and away from open, presence-based coaching. With a specialist therapist, you build a diagram on paper that links the situations where a learning seems to have formed, as far as you remember them, the emotional rule learned there, the danger the rule predicts, and the symptom that guards against that danger. The map then becomes the plan for finding and testing a contradiction.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing the whole logic of a symptom laid out link by link is meant to make it feel understandable rather than random, and to show exactly which link needs a vivid counterexample.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over several structured sessions you and the therapist fill in a printed map with four boxes, revising each until it feels emotionally true, not just logical, and the work can get intense as old feelings rise. Once the map is complete, the therapist helps you find an experience, recent or remembered, that contradicts the key rule and has you hold the rule and the contradiction in mind together. You keep the map and mark any links that still feel true for the next session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think visually or analytically, who like to see how things fit together, and who want structure while doing deep emotional work.
modalities.cautions: Untested and specialist-only, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care: the map is filled in only from memories you already have, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and a neat diagram is not evidence of what happened. Filling it in can stir strong feelings, so the therapist leaves time to settle, and it should not replace well-tested treatments without professional advice.
modalities.tweet: Proposed method: the Symptom Logic Map. With a therapist you draw four linked boxes: an early experience, the rule it taught you, the danger that rule predicts, and the symptom guarding against it. Then you hunt for a counterexample. For visual thinkers.

modalities.name: Audit Every Trigger
modalities.tagline: Systematically checking every old trigger to see what has really changed.
modalities.whatItIs: Audit Every Trigger is a proposed specialist protocol that takes the final checking step of emotional-learning work and makes it the center of the method, the opposite of practices that drop all control and intention. After deep work on a symptom's roots, therapist and client draw up a full list of situations that used to set it off and test each one in a fixed order. Anything that still triggers the old reaction goes straight back into the work.
modalities.coreIdea: Change in an old emotional learning should show up as triggers that no longer bite, so a strict, written audit of every trigger is meant to separate real change from hope or politeness.
modalities.whatYouDo: With your therapist you list ten to twenty old triggers, such as a critical email or a partner's raised voice, and rate how strongly each used to hit. In set sessions you revisit each one in imagination and, where safe, in planned real-life situations together with a trusted friend or partner who has agreed to come along and afterwards says what they noticed, and you rate what you feel now. Triggers that still fire are traced back to the learning that is left, and the audit is repeated a few weeks later.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have done deep work on a pattern and want an honest, structured way to see what has shifted and what has not.
modalities.cautions: This untested protocol is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care and works mostly with present-day triggers; any old memories that come up are ones you already have, are not evidence of what happened and are never pursued to uncover forgotten events. Triggers are revisited from mild to strong and stopped if distress gets too high, real-life checks never involve unsafe people or situations, and people with severe trauma or a current crisis need stabilization first.
modalities.tweet: How do you know an old pattern has really shifted? Proposed: Audit Every Trigger. You and a therapist list every situation that used to set it off and test each one, mild to strong. Whatever still bites goes back into the work. An honest check.

modalities.name: Someone Who Was There
modalities.tagline: Someone who shared those years keeps you company while you feel them.
modalities.whatItIs: Someone Who Was There is a proposed format that moves emotional-learning work away from silent, solitary observation and toward live, spoken company. Once you have named an old emotional learning with a specialist therapist, such as 'I was alone with everything', a willing person who shared that time, such as a sibling or an old family friend, joins one session to sit with you while you feel it. They speak only about their own experience, never as a judge of yours, so their presence, not their memories, is meant to offer the contrast.
modalities.coreIdea: An old learning of being alone may meet a live contradiction when someone who shared those years simply stays with you while you feel it, without either of you needing to agree on what happened.
modalities.whatYouDo: The therapist first meets the visitor alone to prepare them, check how that time affected them too and offer them support of their own, and both of you agree that nothing said leaves the room without the other's consent. In a joint 90-minute session you share the old learning in a sentence and the visitor speaks only about their own experience of those years, never correcting or confirming yours, while the therapist helps you notice what it is like not to be alone with it. A follow-up session without the visitor looks at what has shifted and plans how to handle any family questions afterwards.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry an old sense of having been alone with something, and who still have a safe, willing person from that time who wants to come.
modalities.cautions: This untested format is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care: both of you speak only from memories you already have, the two accounts are not evidence of what happened or corrections of each other, and the session is never used to uncover forgotten events. A visitor joins only when safe and voluntary, never anyone involved in abuse, the session stops if it turns into blame or dismissal, and because it can stir loyalty conflicts or family fallout, you and the therapist plan beforehand what, if anything, is shared outside.
modalities.tweet: Concept for an old feeling of being alone: Someone Who Was There. A safe person who shared those years, like a sibling, joins one session with a trauma-trained therapist, not to correct your memories but to sit with you while you feel it.

modalities.name: Small Steps Down
modalities.tagline: Reaching the deepest roots of a pattern in small, calm steps.
modalities.whatItIs: Small Steps Down is a new, untested concept for doing deep emotional-learning work at the lowest possible intensity, the far opposite of all-out, high-adrenaline effort. A specialist therapist approaches the earliest roots of a pattern one small piece at a time, keeping you calm and settled throughout. The structure is loose and the pace is set by how steady you feel, not by a plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Deep material may be reached more safely in small doses, with frequent returns to calm, so each step down is followed by settling before going any further.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 50-minute session starts and ends with ten minutes of calm conversation about the present, and in between you spend only a few minutes with one small piece of an old feeling or a memory you already have, often from a safe distance, such as describing it as if seen through a window. If your stress rises, you stop and settle before choosing whether to go on. Over many weeks the small pieces add up toward the learning behind the pattern.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to work with deep, early roots but are wary of being overwhelmed, including those who have found intense therapies too much.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea that only a licensed clinician trained in trauma care should lead: each small step uses a feeling or a memory you already have, never a search for forgotten events, and images that arise are not evidence of what happened. Slow does not mean risk-free, so the therapist watches for signs of overwhelm or dissociation, and it should not replace well-tested trauma treatments without professional advice.
modalities.tweet: A gentle new concept: Small Steps Down. With a trauma-trained therapist, deep work on a pattern's roots happens only a few minutes at a time, from a safe distance, with plenty of calm before and after. Slow, and still carefully watched 🪶

modalities.name: Writing Back to the Rule
modalities.tagline: A written dialogue with an old rule, guided by a therapist.
modalities.whatItIs: Writing Back to the Rule is a proposed solitary, written method that pushes emotional-learning work as far from team play and real-time interaction as it can go. Alone, at your own pace, you write in the voice of an old emotional rule, explaining why your symptom is needed, and then write back to it from what you know now. A specialist therapist reads every letter and replies in writing with prompts for the next one.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving an old emotional learning its own voice on paper, and answering it, is meant to bring it fully into awareness and set it next to contradicting knowledge, slowly and privately.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you spend 30 to 45 minutes alone writing a letter in the voice of the rule, for example 'I keep you busy because if you stop, you'll feel how alone you were'. A day or two later you write a reply from your adult self with what you have since learned, and you send both through a secure channel to your therapist. The therapist responds in writing with questions and suggestions, and you meet by video once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who express themselves better in writing than out loud, who live far from specialist help, or who find face-to-face emotional work too exposing.
modalities.cautions: Because this is an untested idea, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care who reads every letter, and the letters draw only on memories you already have: what you write, and the images and feelings it stirs, are not evidence of what happened, and writing is never used to dig for forgotten events. Your therapist checks in regularly with a clear plan if a letter shows distress or risk, letters are kept private and secure, and people with severe trauma or a current crisis need in-person care.
modalities.tweet: Concept for people who say it better in writing: Writing Back to the Rule. Alone, you write in the voice of an old emotional rule ('I keep you busy because...') and then write back. A therapist reads both and replies with prompts for the next round ✉️

modalities.name: Past Its Expiry Date
modalities.tagline: Finding the date when an old emotional rule stopped being true.
modalities.whatItIs: Past Its Expiry Date is a new, untested concept that turns away from the endurance model of change, where you keep pushing until a new habit wins, and instead asks when an old rule stopped applying. With a specialist therapist, you work out the conditions that made an old emotional learning sensible, such as 'stay quiet or things get worse', and then pin down the point in your life when those conditions ended. The rule is seen as an expired document that is still being obeyed.
modalities.coreIdea: Many old learnings were accurate for the place and time they were formed, so finding the moment their conditions ended is meant to give a precise, felt contradiction: the rule was true then, and it is out of date now.
modalities.whatYouDo: In structured sessions you write the rule as one sentence, list in plain words the conditions that made it true, such as living with an unpredictable adult, and mark on a page when each condition ended, using what you already remember. The therapist then asks you to feel the rule's pull while looking at its expiry date, saying aloud 'this was true until...'. Later sessions check whether the rule still grips in today's situations that resemble the old ones.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know their reactions belong to another time and place but still feel them, and who like clear, structured steps.
modalities.cautions: As an untested idea, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care: the conditions and dates come only from memories you already have, the images and feelings they bring are not evidence of what happened, and they are never pursued to uncover forgotten events. Some conditions, such as ongoing danger at home, have not ended, and then safety comes first and this method does not apply.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical approach: Past Its Expiry Date. With a trauma-trained therapist you work out the conditions that made an old rule true ('stay quiet or things get worse') and when they ended, then feel its pull next to that date. True then, out of date now.

modalities.name: Help That Was Safe
modalities.tagline: Starting from a time, past or recent, when being helped was safe.
modalities.whatItIs: Help That Was Safe is a proposed deep, specialist-led method for people ruled by the learning that they must always be strong and never need anyone. Rather than tracing the rule itself, it starts from a counterexample: a time, long ago or last week, when you were helped, held or let off the hook and it was safe. The work is loose and accepting, and that experience is explored slowly until it can stand next to the rule.
modalities.coreIdea: A rule like 'I must never be weak' is contradicted by any real experience of being safely helped, so the practice is to find one such experience and let it become vivid enough to sit beside the rule.
modalities.whatYouDo: In unhurried weekly sessions the therapist asks whether any time comes to mind, from long ago or from this month, when someone helped you and nothing bad followed, such as a neighbor driving you to hospital or a colleague covering a shift; if nothing does, you watch for one in the coming week. You describe it slowly, what you saw, felt and expected, while the therapist helps you notice the part of you that still braces against it. When it feels vivid, you hold it alongside the old rule and notice what happens to the rule.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never ask for help, who push through illness and grief alone, or who feel shame at any sign of weakness, and who sense this is costing them.
modalities.cautions: Untested so far, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care and starts from experiences you already have, past or recent; images and feelings that arise are not evidence of what happened, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten events. For some people even good experiences stir grief, and it should not replace well-tested treatments for depression or trauma without professional advice.
modalities.tweet: Never ask for help? A new idea: Help That Was Safe. With a trauma-trained therapist, you slowly explore one real time, past or recent, when someone helped you and it was safe, and let it sit beside the rule that you must never seem weak.

modalities.name: The Dream Doorway
modalities.tagline: Using a recurring dream as the way into an old emotional learning.
modalities.whatItIs: The Dream Doorway is a new, untested concept that moves emotional-learning work as far as possible from real, present-moment contact, such as time with an animal, into pure inner imagery. It uses a dream that keeps coming back, such as being chased or missing an exam, as a vivid starting point for finding what an old learning predicts. A specialist therapist guides the work one to one.
modalities.coreIdea: A recurring dream can carry the same mood as a waking symptom, and matching that mood to real situations, rather than decoding symbols, is meant to bring the shared emotional expectation into awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: You keep a brief dream note by your bed, and in sessions you describe the overall mood of a recurring dream in a few words, such as 'trapped and late'. With the therapist you then list the waking situations that carry the same mood, and look across them for the expectation they share, for example 'whatever I do, I'll fall short'. The therapist helps you find knowledge that contradicts that expectation and has you feel both together.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with vivid recurring dreams, who are curious about what they might connect to, and who find imagery easier to work with than direct talk.
modalities.cautions: This untested idea is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, works only with dreams and memories you already have, and never takes a dream, or the images and feelings it brings, as evidence of what happened or uses it to uncover forgotten events. Nightmares that disturb sleep also call for a check with a doctor, and anyone whose dreams replay a traumatic event should first be assessed by a trauma-focused clinician.
modalities.tweet: Recurring dream of being chased or missing an exam? A speculative idea: The Dream Doorway. With a therapist you name the dream's mood ('trapped and late'), find the waking situations that feel the same, and look for the expectation they share.

modalities.name: Vivid but Bearable
modalities.tagline: Feeling an old learning vividly, but always within what you can bear.
modalities.whatItIs: Vivid but Bearable is a proposed method that moves emotional-learning work away from calm, gentle, body-centered practice toward clearly felt emotion, while keeping it within what you can tolerate. It is based on the view that an old emotional learning needs to be felt, not just talked about, for a contradiction to reach it, but it always stays well short of overwhelming and never aims at release. A specialist therapist keeps the feeling vivid enough to be real and small enough to stay manageable.
modalities.coreIdea: An old learning may only meet a contradiction when it is actually felt, so the work aims for a clear, bearable dose of the old feeling, with the contradiction ready, rather than as much feeling as possible.
modalities.whatYouDo: After several sessions of preparation, in which you agree on stop signals, a 0 to 10 scale for how strong the feeling may get (usually no higher than 5) and ways to settle, the therapist helps you recall a present-day trigger until the old feeling is clearly there. While it is felt, the therapist brings in the contradicting knowledge you prepared together and asks you to notice both at once, turning the feeling down whenever it climbs past the agreed level. Every session ends with at least 15 minutes of settling and talk about the present.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who understand a pattern in their heads but have never let themselves feel what is under it, and who have the stability and support for emotional work.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, led only by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care and starting from present-day triggers and memories you already have; nothing that arises is evidence of what happened, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. It is only for people screened as stable, not for anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder, a heart condition made worse by stress, or a current crisis, and intensity is never pushed past what you can bear.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Vivid but Bearable. Only after screening and with a trauma-trained clinician, you let an old feeling be clearly felt, never past an agreed level, while holding what you know now beside it. Knowing a pattern is not the same as feeling it.

modalities.name: Two Clips, One Voice
modalities.tagline: Hearing your own voice state the old rule, then what's true now.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Clips, One Voice is a new, untested concept that turns emotional-learning work into a structured, solitary listening practice, the opposite of everyday sociable connection. In session, with a specialist therapist, you record two short clips in your own voice: one stating the old emotional rule as you feel it, one stating what you now know that contradicts it. Between sessions you listen to them back to back, alone, at set times.
modalities.coreIdea: Hearing your own voice say the old rule and then its contradiction, one straight after the other, is meant to keep both in awareness together, which is when an old learning is thought to be most open to change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Near the end of a session, once the rule and the contradicting knowledge are clear, you record each in about 30 seconds, for example 'if I stop being useful, people will drop me' followed by 'my friends stayed when I was ill and useless for months'. For two weeks you listen to the pair twice a day, alone, noting in one line how true the first clip feels. You bring the notes to the next session, where the therapist adjusts or re-records the clips.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like structure and private practice, who are already working with a specialist, and who find their own voice more convincing than anyone else's.
modalities.cautions: This untested practice is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, who records the clips with you in session: they draw only on present-day rules and memories you already have, what you feel while listening is not evidence of what happened, and the clips are never used to uncover forgotten events. Keep the clips short and private, and stop listening and contact your therapist if they bring up strong distress, trauma memories or thoughts of harming yourself.
modalities.tweet: Prototype: Two Clips, One Voice. In session you record the old rule in your own voice ('if I stop being useful, people will drop me') and then what you know now. At home you play them back to back, twice a day, with your therapist checking in.

modalities.name: Clocked Unlocking
modalities.tagline: A strict, clocked sequence: wake the old feeling, then surprise it.
modalities.whatItIs: Clocked Unlocking is a proposed indoor protocol that pushes emotional-learning work as far as possible toward structure and precision, the opposite of an open, wandering walk outdoors. It borrows a hypothesis from laboratory research on memory: that a reactivated emotional memory may be open to revision for a limited time afterwards. A specialist therapist runs a fixed, clocked sequence of reactivation, contradiction and checking within that window.
modalities.coreIdea: If timing matters when an emotional memory is revised, then waking the old learning and bringing in a vivid contradiction within the same short, planned window is meant to give the contradiction its best chance to register.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session follows the same script: five minutes recalling a recent moment when the old learning fired, until it is clearly felt, then, within about ten minutes, a prepared contradicting experience held alongside it, repeated three times with short pauses. The therapist times each step and you rate how true the old learning feels at the start and the end. Sessions finish with settling time, and the whole protocol is reviewed together after four weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like clear, step-by-step methods with something to measure, and who want deep emotional work to feel precise rather than open-ended.
modalities.cautions: An untested protocol led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, built on recent moments and memories you already have: what is recalled, including any images and feelings, is not evidence of what happened, and the sequence is never used to uncover forgotten events. The laboratory timing findings have not been shown to apply to therapy, so this is a hypothesis to test, not a proven recipe, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis need stabilization first.
modalities.tweet: Experimental protocol: Clocked Unlocking. Lab research suggests a reawakened emotional memory may be briefly open to change, so a therapist runs a strict, clocked sequence: feel the old rule, then meet a contradiction within minutes. A hypothesis to test.

modalities.name: Unwritten House Rules
modalities.tagline: Finding the unwritten emotional rules your family taught you.
modalities.whatItIs: Unwritten House Rules is a new, untested concept that moves emotional-learning work away from plain sensing of the present and toward the remembered emotional climate of the family you grew up in. A specialist therapist helps you name the unwritten rules that still steer your reactions, such as 'anger is dangerous' or 'needs are a burden'. You work one to one with the therapist, and the rules are seen as patterns you sense, not facts to prove.
modalities.coreIdea: Many present-day reactions may follow rules absorbed from family life long before they could be questioned, and naming those rules as rules is meant to make them visible enough to be contradicted.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over several sessions you and the therapist write a short list of the unspoken emotional rules you sense from your family life, each with a present-day moment when it still fires and, only if one comes to mind easily, a remembered example. For the rule that bites hardest, the therapist helps you feel its pull at a level you can bear and then find experiences, now or remembered, that clearly break it. You keep the list and mark which rules still grip as the weeks go on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice they react like their parents did, or who grew up with strong unspoken rules about feelings, and who want to understand where their reactions come from.
modalities.cautions: Led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, this untested idea takes its rules only from memories you already have and patterns you sense now: family images and feelings that arise are not evidence of what happened, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten events. Naming family rules can stir grief, anger or guilt toward people you love, so the work stays on how each rule affects you now rather than on blaming or confronting relatives, and anyone still living in an unsafe home needs safety support first.
modalities.tweet: Some of your reactions may follow rules your family never said out loud ('anger is dangerous', 'needs are a burden'). A new concept: Unwritten House Rules. With a therapist, you write those rules down, see which still fire, and look for proof against them.

modalities.name: The Joyless Promise
modalities.tagline: Uncovering a hidden promise that forbids you to enjoy life.
modalities.whatItIs: The Joyless Promise is a proposed, specialist-led method that turns away from simply adding enjoyable things, such as music, to a hard life, and asks whether enjoyment is being blocked by an old, unspoken promise. Such promises are often made out of loyalty, for example 'I won't be happy while my mother is unhappy' or 'having fun would betray those who struggled'. The work is structured, quiet and one to one.
modalities.coreIdea: Guilt around pleasure can come from a loyal promise made long ago, and bringing that promise into words, and asking whether the person it was for would want it kept, is meant to give it a vivid contradiction.
modalities.whatYouDo: In structured weekly sessions, you recall a recent good moment that turned to guilt, and the therapist helps you complete the sentence 'if I let myself enjoy this, I would be...', until a promise comes into words, such as 'leaving my brother behind'. You say the promise aloud and feel its weight, then the therapist asks what that person, at their kindest, would actually want for you. You hold both together and notice how the next good moment feels.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty when life goes well, especially when someone close to them has struggled, been ill or died.
modalities.cautions: Untested so far, it is led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care and works only from good moments and memories you already have: images and feelings that arise are not evidence of what happened, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. Losing the ability to enjoy anything for weeks can be a sign of depression, which should be assessed by a doctor or therapist, and work involving grief needs careful pacing.
