modalities.tweet: Feel guilty when life goes well? A new idea: The Joyless Promise. With a therapist you find the old, loyal promise behind it ('I won't be happy while she isn't') and ask what that person, at their kindest, would want for you.

modalities.name: Eyes on the Room
modalities.tagline: Letting your legs tremble while staying in touch with the room.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyes on the Room is a new, untested concept that pushes tremor-based practice as far as possible from inner imagery, memory and guidance. After tiring the legs until they begin to tremble, you let the tremor run with your eyes open, keeping your attention on what you can actually see, hear and touch right now. It is fully self-led, present-focused and allowing: nothing is pictured, remembered or worked on.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying oriented to the real surroundings while the body shakes is meant to keep the practice grounded in the present and stop it drifting into old memories or imagined scenes.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few minutes of easy movement to warm up, you do about 12 minutes of leg-tiring exercises, such as wall sits, slow lunges and calf raises, until your thighs feel tired and a little shaky. Then you lie on a mat with knees bent and eyes open, letting the legs tremble for up to 15 minutes while you silently name things you see on the ceiling, sounds in the room and the feel of the floor under your back. You stop at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift into memories or worry when they close their eyes, and who want a simple, physical way to unwind that keeps them anchored in the here and now.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and stop the leg exercises at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. During the tremor, stop if you feel pain, panic or overwhelm, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder or another serious mental health condition should learn tremor practices only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Eyes on the Room. Tire your legs with a few wall sits, lie down, and let them tremble while you keep your eyes open and name what you see and hear. Body busy, mind in the room. Doctor check first, and stop if it gets too much.

modalities.name: Hands That Feel It
modalities.tagline: Resting your own hands on your body to feel the tremor directly.
modalities.whatItIs: Hands That Feel It is a proposed self-led variation of tremor-based practice that keeps attention entirely on direct physical contact, the opposite of inner work with imagined figures or parts. While the legs tremble, you place your own hands, in a set order, on the thighs, belly and chest to feel the movement under your palms. It is calm, structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling the tremor through your own hands gives the mind one simple, present thing to follow, which is meant to make the practice steadier and more settling than watching it from inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a short warm-up and ten to fifteen minutes of leg-tiring exercises, you lie on your back with knees bent and let the tremor start. You then rest your hands for three minutes each on your thighs, your lower belly and the center of your chest, simply feeling the tremor or stillness under your palms, and finish with both hands on the belly for a few slow breaths. A session takes about 30 minutes, and you can stop at any point by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body practices too vague or floaty, who like having something concrete to do, and who find steady touch comforting.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and ease off and stop the tiring exercises if you notice chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Strong emotions can surface during tremor practice, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who finds body practices too vague, an idea: tire your legs, lie down, let them tremble, and rest your own hands on your thighs, belly and chest to feel it under your palms. Calm, simple, something concrete to hold on to. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: Nothing Has to Happen
modalities.tagline: A tremor practice with no goal, no counting and no right result.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing Has to Happen is a new, untested concept that takes tremor-based practice as far as possible from goal-setting, tracking and deliberate change. You tire the legs and lie down, but you do not try to make a tremor start, last or feel a certain way. Whatever the body does, whether shaking, stillness, yawning, sighing or sleepiness, is equally welcome.
modalities.coreIdea: Trying hard to get a 'good' session can turn a body practice into another task to fail at, so dropping every target is meant to leave the body free to do whatever it does.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a couple of minutes of easy movement to warm up, you do whichever leg-tiring exercises feel right that day for ten minutes or so, then lie down on a mat or rug, knees bent, for as long as you like. If a tremor comes, you let it; if it does not, you simply rest, with nothing to focus on and nothing to achieve. You keep no log and give no ratings, and you stop whenever you have had enough by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side.
modalities.whoItsFor: Perfectionists and people who turn every practice into a performance, and anyone who wants a body practice that asks nothing of them.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and even with no targets the tiring part is real effort, so stop it for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Feelings or memories can surface while lying still, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Nothing Has to Happen. Tire your legs a little, lie down, and let the body do whatever it does: tremble, rest, yawn, nothing at all. No goal, no counting, no right result. Even relaxing doesn't have to be a test 🌿

modalities.name: Tremor in Color
modalities.tagline: Drawing where the tremor went, session after session, without words.
modalities.whatItIs: Tremor in Color is a proposed solitary variation of tremor-based practice that moves even further from talk, values and mental exercises than the original. After each session you color a simple outline of a body to show where you felt tremor, tension or warmth, without writing a single word. Over weeks, the maps build a private, picture-only record of how your body responds.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping the record in pictures rather than words is meant to keep attention on the body itself, and the growing pile of maps may show patterns that a diary of thoughts would miss.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you do a structured 30-minute session: a three-minute warm-up, 12 minutes of set leg-tiring exercises, up to 15 minutes lying down letting the tremor run (ended at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side), then two minutes with colored pencils and a printed body outline. You use one color for tremor, one for tension and one for ease, and date the page. Every month you lay the maps side by side and simply look, without analyzing.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of talking about their feelings, who think visually, or who want to notice how their body changes over time without keeping a diary.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and the maps are a personal record, not a medical test, so see a doctor about any new pain, numbness or unusual shaking, and check with a doctor before starting if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries. Stop the exercises for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness and the tremor if you feel overwhelmed or spaced out, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: Concept: after each body-shaking session, you color a simple body outline to show where you felt tremor, tension or ease. No words at all. Over weeks the maps become a picture diary of your body, no talking required.

modalities.name: Just Tired Muscles
modalities.tagline: Tired muscles shake, and that is all it needs to mean.
modalities.whatItIs: Just Tired Muscles is a new, untested concept that strips tremor-based practice of every story about trauma, energy or hidden meaning, the opposite of approaches that search for the emotional truth behind a symptom. It explains the shaking simply as what tired muscles do, and invites you to enjoy it as a calming, physical experience. It is self-led, quiet and present-focused.
modalities.coreIdea: You do not need to believe that shaking releases anything for it to feel pleasant and settling, so the practice keeps the experience and drops the theory.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a minute or two of easy marching to warm up, you tire your legs with a few minutes of wall sits and slow squats until they feel shaky, then lie down with knees bent for ten to fifteen minutes and let them tremble. If your mind starts looking for meaning ('what is coming out of me?'), you remind yourself 'these are tired muscles' and go back to the plain feel of the movement. You can end the tremor at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and afterwards you rest for a few minutes before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: Skeptics who like the feel of shaking practices but not the claims around them, and anyone who wants a simple, calming wind-down with nothing to interpret.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and stop the wall sits and squats if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Even without any story, strong feelings can surface, so pause if you feel overwhelmed or in pain, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: A skeptic-friendly idea: Just Tired Muscles. Tire your legs, lie down, let them tremble. No talk of releasing trauma or energy, just tired muscles doing what tired muscles do. The shaking, without the claims.

modalities.name: Upright Tremble
modalities.tagline: Letting the tremor run while standing, eyes open, holding a wall.
modalities.whatItIs: Upright Tremble is a proposed active variation of tremor-based practice that moves away from slow, inward, still attention and toward standing, outward, physical engagement. Instead of lying down after the tiring exercises, you stay on your feet, holding a wall or sturdy chair, and let the tremor run through bent knees and hips. It is structured, a little more energetic than lying practice, and learned from a trained provider.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the body shake while upright and alert is meant to link the tremor with everyday standing life, so the practice feels active and outward rather than inward and sleepy.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few minutes of easy warm-up and 15 minutes of set leg-tiring exercises, you stand with feet hip-width apart, one hand on a wall, and soften your knees until a tremor starts in the thighs. For up to ten minutes you let it run, adjusting the bend of your knees to make it gentler or stronger, and straightening them or sitting on the chair beside you to stop it at any moment, with eyes open and attention on staying balanced and upright. You finish by standing still for a minute, then walking slowly around the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get sleepy or lost in thought lying down, who prefer to stay on their feet, and who like a more energetic, outward-facing practice.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: shaking while standing carries a risk of losing balance, so always hold a wall or sturdy chair, keep the area clear, and sit down at once if you feel chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or overwhelm. Check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures, heart, balance or joint problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a shaking practice you do on your feet: tire your legs, hold a wall, soften your knees and let the tremor run while you look around the room. A new, more upright take for people who get sleepy or lost in thought lying down. Hold on to something!

modalities.name: Rung by Rung
modalities.tagline: A self-coached, step-by-step plan for building a home shaking practice.
modalities.whatItIs: Rung by Rung is a new, untested concept that turns tremor-based practice into a structured, self-run progression, the opposite of open, presence-based coaching. A printed plan sets out eight weekly rungs, each adding a little more tremor time or a new position, with clear rules for when to stay on a rung. You follow it alone and judge your own progress against simple checks.
modalities.coreIdea: Building up gradually and predictably is meant to make a home shaking practice safer and easier to keep, because you always know the next small step and when to hold back.
modalities.whatYouDo: In week one you warm up for a few minutes, do the tiring exercises and allow just three minutes of tremor, three times a week, ending it by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side; each week adds two or three minutes or a new variation, such as feet flat or knees wider. You move up a rung only if the last week felt comfortable, and drop back one rung after any session that left you shaky, tearful or wired. A short checklist after each session records time, comfort and anything to watch.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like plans and gradual progress, who want to practice at home without a teacher every week, and who appreciate clear rules for going slowly.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, and the usual advice is to learn tremor practices first with a certified provider, and only with a clinically trained one if you have severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder. Check with a doctor before starting if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and end any session at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness, or if you feel overwhelmed or spaced out.
modalities.tweet: A proposal for building a home shaking practice: Rung by Rung. Start with three minutes of tremor, add a little each week, and drop back a rung whenever a session leaves you wired or teary. Slow and steady, on purpose.

modalities.name: Dial the Tremor
modalities.tagline: Training yourself to turn a tremor up, down and off on cue.
modalities.whatItIs: Dial the Tremor is a proposed precise, provider-taught variation of tremor-based practice that makes control the whole point, the far opposite of letting go of all intention. You learn to raise, lower and stop the tremor at set moments by changing leg position, like turning a dimmer switch. Sessions follow an exact script with counts and timings.
modalities.coreIdea: Being able to turn a body reaction up and down on purpose is meant to build a felt sense of being in charge of it, which may make the practice feel safer and more predictable.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a short warm-up and the standard tiring exercises, you lie down and follow a timed script, often with a provider counting: one minute of gentle tremor with knees close together, one minute stronger with knees apart, thirty seconds stopped with legs straight, then repeat four times. You rate how well you could match each level on a simple 0 to 3 scale. Once you can follow the script reliably, you practice it at home twice a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel uneasy letting the body move on its own, who want to know they can stop at any moment, and who like precise, measurable practice.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and stop the tiring exercises for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Learn it with a clinically trained provider if you have severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder, and whatever the script says, straighten your legs or roll onto your side to stop at once if you feel pain, panic or spaced out.
modalities.tweet: Speculative twist on body shaking: Dial the Tremor. You learn to turn the tremor up, down and off on cue by moving your knees, following a timed script. Less 'let go', more 'I'm in charge'. Doctor check first, and learn it with a trained provider.

modalities.name: Sigh and Tremble
modalities.tagline: Letting sighs, hums and sounds out as the body shakes.
modalities.whatItIs: Sigh and Tremble is a proposed variation of tremor-based practice that moves away from silent, still observation and lets the voice join in. While the legs tremble, you allow long sighs, hums or soft sounds to come out with the breath instead of keeping quiet. It is a little more active and expressive than plain tremor practice, and is learned from a provider.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting breath and voice move with the body, rather than holding them still while watching, is meant to make the practice feel fuller and less controlled.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a short warm-up and 15 minutes of tiring exercises, you lie down with knees bent and let the tremor start, then breathe out through the mouth in long sighs, adding a soft hum or 'ahh' whenever it feels natural. You do not perform or force sounds; you simply stop holding them back, for up to 15 minutes. You can stop at any point by straightening your legs, and you end with a minute of quiet breathing before rolling onto your side to get up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold their breath or clench their jaw when stressed, who find silent practice tense, and who have a private space where they can make some noise.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: forced or very deep breathing can cause dizziness or tingling, so keep sighs relaxed and stop if you feel lightheaded or overwhelmed, and stop the tiring exercises for chest pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures, heart or breathing problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: Do you hold your breath when stressed? An idea: Sigh and Tremble. Tire your legs, lie down, let them shake, and let long sighs and soft hums out with the breath. A louder, looser body practice for people who clench their jaw and keep everything in.

modalities.name: The Resting Quiver
modalities.tagline: A near-effortless tremor practice for a bed, sofa or armchair.
modalities.whatItIs: The Resting Quiver is a new, untested concept that strips tremor-based practice of almost all effort, the far opposite of hard, fast interval training. There are no wall sits or lunges: a few minutes of gentle, held positions in bed or a chair are used to invite a soft quiver, and the aim is to stay as calm and unhurried as possible. It is loosely structured, very allowing, and learned from a provider who adapts it to your body.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people cannot or should not do vigorous tiring exercises, so the practice looks for the smallest, softest way into a settling tremor, with calm as the priority throughout.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying in bed or sitting well supported in an armchair, you gently press your knees together for a minute, let go, then rest your feet flat and let the knees drift slightly apart, noticing any small quiver in the thighs. If one comes, you let it run softly for a few minutes, stopping it whenever you like by stretching your legs out or rolling onto your side; if not, you simply rest and breathe slowly. A session takes 10 to 20 minutes and can end in sleep or rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with low energy, limited mobility, long-term illness or older bodies who find standard exercises too demanding, and anyone who wants the calmest possible version.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea that still invites tremor, so adapt it with a provider and check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures, a neurological or heart condition, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries; new or unexplained shaking should always be checked by a doctor rather than practiced with. Stop if you feel unwell or overwhelmed, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Untested and gentle: The Resting Quiver, a shaking practice with almost no effort. No wall sits, just gentle held positions in bed or an armchair, a soft quiver if it comes, and lots of rest. Adapt it with a provider, and get any new shaking checked.

modalities.name: Last Light Unwinding
modalities.tagline: A quiet, solitary shaking routine for the last twenty minutes before sleep.
modalities.whatItIs: Last Light Unwinding is a proposed solitary, night-time version of tremor-based practice, the opposite of loud, competitive, sociable sport. It uses only gentle tiring movements and a dim, quiet room, and ends in bed with the lights off. A provider helps you set it up, and while the start time stays fixed, the moves can change with how the day went.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing the same gentle, calming body routine alone at the end of every day is meant to signal to the body that the day is over and make the shift toward sleep feel easier.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twenty minutes before bed, with lights low and phone in another room, you do five minutes of slow calf raises and gentle knee bends, then lie on your bed with knees bent and let any light tremor run for up to ten minutes. When it fades, or sooner if you choose, you stretch out your legs to end it, pull up the blanket and breathe slowly until you are ready to sleep. On restless nights you can swap in other gentle moves the provider has shown you, but the start time stays the same.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who lie awake replaying the day, who come home wired from busy, social or noisy days, and who like a simple, private bedtime ritual.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and not a sleep treatment, so ongoing insomnia, loud snoring or daytime sleepiness should be checked by a doctor, as should epilepsy or seizures, heart problems, pregnancy, or recent surgery, fractures or injuries before you start. Strong emotions can surface when lying still, so if bedtime tremor stirs things up, move it earlier, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Imagined bedtime ritual: Last Light Unwinding. Lights low, phone away, five minutes of gentle calf raises, then lie down and let any soft tremor run until it fades. A quiet end to a day you keep replaying 🌙

modalities.name: Counted Out-Breaths
modalities.tagline: Slow, counted out-breaths paced through a gentle body tremor.
modalities.whatItIs: Counted Out-Breaths is a new, untested concept that pairs tremor-based practice with slow, counted breathing, turning away from long, continuous effort toward short, calm, structured sessions. During the tremor phase you breathe out for longer than you breathe in, following a set count taught by a provider. The tiring phase is light, so the whole session stays gentle.
modalities.coreIdea: Slow breathing with long out-breaths is widely used to settle the body, and pacing the breath through a gentle tremor is meant to give the practice a steady, calming rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: A provider first teaches you the routine in one or two sessions, and you then practice at home. After five minutes of light tiring exercises, you lie down, let a gentle tremor start, and breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six or seven, for ten minutes. You can stop the tremor at any point by straightening your legs, you finish with two minutes of normal breathing, and you check in with the provider once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel keyed up and want a very calm, structured routine, and who find it easier to settle when they have a breathing count to follow.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: stop if counting the breath makes you anxious, dizzy or short of breath, and check with a doctor first if you have asthma, lung or heart conditions, epilepsy or seizures, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries. People with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: A new pairing: Counted Out-Breaths. A light leg tremor plus slow counted breathing, in for four and out for six or seven, for ten calm minutes. For keyed-up people who settle more easily with a count to follow than with 'just relax'.

modalities.name: Tears Are Welcome
modalities.tagline: A gentle tremor practice where tears, sighs or laughter are welcome.
modalities.whatItIs: Tears Are Welcome is a proposed variation of tremor-based practice that drops the effortful push of strength-style exercise and makes emotional permission its center. With only light leg movements, you let a gentle tremor run and allow any feeling that comes with it, whether tears, laughter, sighs or nothing at all, without stopping it or explaining it. A provider teaches it together with a simple aftercare plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people brace against feelings as hard as they brace their muscles, so pairing a soft tremor with explicit permission to feel, and a plan for afterwards, is meant to make emotion less something to hold back.
modalities.whatYouDo: After five minutes of light leg movements, you lie down with a blanket and tissues nearby and let a gentle tremor run for up to 15 minutes, ending it whenever you wish by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and letting any feeling move through without telling yourself a story about it. Afterwards you follow your aftercare plan: a warm drink, a few minutes sitting up, and a message to a person you trust if you want one. You meet the provider every two weeks to talk about how it is going.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold back tears or feelings until they are exhausted, and who want a soft, private way to let them move, with a plan for afterwards.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events: any memory that comes up is one you already had, and the images and feelings with it are not evidence of what happened. If strong emotions, memories or a sense of unreality come up, stop and contact your provider, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder or a current crisis should practice only with a clinically trained provider alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: Here's a softer idea: Tears Are Welcome. A light leg routine, a gentle tremor on the floor, and open permission for whatever comes with it (tears, laughter, nothing), plus a plan for afterwards. Holding it all in becomes optional.

modalities.name: Suitcase Routine
modalities.tagline: A short, self-run shaking routine that needs no mat, teacher or company.
modalities.whatItIs: Suitcase Routine is a new, untested concept that makes tremor-based practice fully portable and self-reliant, the opposite of sessions built around a trained animal and its handler. It is a fixed, 15-minute routine you can do alone in a hotel room, an office or a quiet corner, with no mat or equipment. Once learned, it needs nobody else.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping one short, memorized routine that fits any floor or chair is meant to let you settle your body wherever you are, without relying on a place, a person or a pet.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a minute of marching on the spot to warm up, you do three set moves for two minutes each, such as calf raises, a wall sit against a solid wall and slow lunges, then sit on a sturdy chair or lie on a towel with knees bent and let a tremor run for up to five minutes, ending it whenever you like by straightening your legs. You finish by standing, shaking out your hands, and taking three slow breaths. It needs only a patch of floor, a wall and a chair or towel, so it works wherever you are.
modalities.whoItsFor: Travelers, shift workers and busy people who want a quick, private way to unwind in any space, without needing a class or another person.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so learn the basics with a certified provider first and check with a doctor if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and stop the moves for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Practicing alone means nobody is there if strong feelings surface, so keep sessions short, stop if you feel overwhelmed or spaced out, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should practice only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: An invented routine for travelers and shift workers: Suitcase Routine. Three moves, two minutes each, then let your legs tremble for up to five minutes on a towel or chair. No mat, no class, no company needed. A portable way to unwind ✈️

modalities.name: Leftover Tiredness
modalities.tagline: Using the tiredness of ordinary days instead of a set exercise form.
modalities.whatItIs: Leftover Tiredness is a proposed loose, unscripted variation of tremor-based practice, moving away from fixed, flowing movement forms. Instead of doing set tiring exercises, you use the natural tiredness your legs already have after a long walk, a day on your feet, climbing stairs or gardening. When it is there, you lie down and let a tremor come.
modalities.coreIdea: Ordinary life already tires the body, so borrowing that tiredness, rather than adding a workout, is meant to fold the practice into the day and keep it simple and flexible.
modalities.whatYouDo: On days when your legs feel heavy, for example after a hike or a long shift, you find ten to twenty minutes, stretch gently for a minute, then lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. You wait for a tremor to start in the thighs and let it run, changing position by feel rather than by a script, and you can end it at any moment by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side. If no tremor comes, you simply rest, and you never add extra effort to force one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already move a lot in daily life, who dislike fixed routines, and who want a flexible practice that fits around real days.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea: do not use it after a fall, an injury or unusual pain, or if the activity that tired you brought chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, all of which need a doctor instead, and check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries. Strong feelings can surface, so stop if you feel overwhelmed, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Novel idea: Leftover Tiredness. Skip the set exercises and use the tiredness life already gave you (a long walk, a day on your feet), then lie down and let your legs tremble. No routine to stick to.

modalities.name: Cool-Down Before Talking
modalities.tagline: A solitary shake-out after a conflict, before going back to talk.
modalities.whatItIs: Cool-Down Before Talking is a new, untested concept that uses tremor-based practice as a fixed, solitary pause after an argument or a tense encounter, the opposite of rushing back into contact. You tell the other person you will be back, go somewhere alone and follow the same short sequence every time before you rejoin the conversation. A provider designs the sequence with you and reviews how it is going every few weeks.
modalities.coreIdea: Agitation after a conflict is partly in the body, so a set routine of effort followed by a settling tremor, done alone, is meant to let you return to the conversation calmer and more able to listen.
modalities.whatYouDo: When a disagreement starts to boil over, you say a pre-agreed line such as 'I need 20 minutes, then I'll come back', go to another room and do a minute of easy marching to warm up, four minutes of brisk leg-tiring moves, ten minutes lying down letting the tremor run and two minutes of slow breathing, ending the tremor sooner by straightening your legs if it feels like too much. Then you return and pick up the conversation, even if you still feel some of the upset. Every few weeks you and the provider look at how the cool-downs went and adjust the steps.
modalities.whoItsFor: Couples, flatmates, parents and colleagues who say things they regret in the heat of an argument, and who want a physical way to pause and come back.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, and stop the brisk moves for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. It is never a way to put up with abuse, threats or violence, which call for safety and specialist support, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: After an argument, try a set routine: 'I need 20 minutes, then I'll come back', a few brisk leg moves, a quiet tremor on the floor, then you return. A new concept: Cool-Down Before Talking, made for the heat of the moment.

modalities.name: Brought to the Mat
modalities.tagline: Holding one recent tense moment in mind while the body trembles.
modalities.whatItIs: Brought to the Mat is a new, untested concept that takes tremor-based practice away from the open, present-only attention of a nature walk and toward a short, set link with your own everyday life. Once a tremor is running, you hold one recent, mildly tense moment in mind for half a minute, then let it go and return to the shaking, following fixed steps and timings. It borrows the pairing of brief recall with a settled body from behavior therapy, but the tremor itself does the settling, and a provider builds the list of moments with you.
modalities.coreIdea: General settling may not reach the particular moments that keep someone tense, so pairing one recent, mildly tense moment with a running tremor, briefly and on a fixed timetable, is meant to let the body practice settling around that moment rather than around stress in general.
modalities.whatYouDo: In two sessions a provider teaches you the exercises and helps you list five recent, everyday moments that left you mildly tense, none above 4 out of 10, such as a curt message or a missed train, with no old or painful memories on the list. At home, after a few minutes of warm-up and the standard tiring exercises, you lie down with knees bent, and once a tremor is running you bring one moment to mind for thirty seconds, let it go and stay with the tremor for five minutes, three rounds in all, ending any round at once by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side. A moment that still feels sharp afterwards comes off the list, and the provider goes over the list with you once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already find tremor practice settling but notice that particular everyday moments, such as a tense call or a crowded commute, stay with them afterwards, and who like clear steps to follow.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea, so check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, stop the warm-up or tiring exercises for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and end any round at once if you feel pain, overwhelm or spaced out. It uses only recent moments you already remember clearly, the images and feelings that come up are not evidence of what happened, it is never used to look for old or forgotten events, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should use it only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Brought to the Mat. While a gentle body tremor runs, you hold one recent, mildly tense moment in mind for 30 seconds, then let it go. For people who settle in general but still carry that curt email around. Everyday moments only, never trauma.

modalities.name: Shake, Then Debrief
modalities.tagline: A tremor session followed by a short, guided look at what surfaced.
modalities.whatItIs: Shake, Then Debrief is a new, untested concept that adds a short, structured debrief to every tremor session, moving away from pure, self-guided sensory attention. After the tiring phase and tremor, you spend five minutes with a card of simple questions about which feelings, images or memories came up, and a trained provider goes through the cards with you every two weeks. Nothing is dug into; the aim is simply to notice and put a few words to it.
modalities.coreIdea: Strong feelings sometimes surface during tremor practice, and a brief, structured debrief with regular support is meant to help you make sense of them gently instead of being left alone with them.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the routine in a few sessions with the provider, you practice alone at home: a few minutes of warm-up, 12 minutes of set tiring exercises and up to 15 minutes of tremor, which you can end at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, then you sit up with a drink of water and answer a short card of questions, such as 'what did I notice?' and 'is there anything I want to leave here?'. Every second week a ten-minute call with the provider goes through your cards and helps you settle anything that stuck. Home practice goes on only while the provider agrees it is going well.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in good health and stable care who notice that shaking practice brings up mild feelings, and who want a short, supported check-in after each session.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and the debrief is not therapy: it notes only what you already noticed, images and feelings that came up are not evidence of what happened, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and if trauma memories come up, the provider pauses home practice and helps you find a trauma-trained clinician. Check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures or heart problems, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, stop the exercises for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should practice only with a clinically trained provider alongside their own treatment.
modalities.tweet: Proposed format: Shake, Then Debrief. Leg exercises and tremor at home, then five minutes with a short debrief card, reviewed with a trained provider every two weeks. Not therapy, just not being left alone with what comes up.

modalities.name: Flights Without a Beat
modalities.tagline: A quiet, solitary tremor after brisk stairs climbed in silence.
modalities.whatItIs: Flights Without a Beat is a new, untested concept that moves tremor-based practice away from rhythm, sound and shared expression and toward silent, solitary effort paced only by your own breath. It replaces the usual floor exercises with a few minutes of brisk stair climbing and a short wall sit at home, until the legs are properly tired. Then you lie down and let the tremor run, with no music, beat or guiding voice.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady, real effort with no beat to follow makes the body set its own pace, and the tiredness it leaves is meant to lead into a settling tremor and a quiet end.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a day, alone and without headphones, you warm up with a minute of easy marching, climb a flight or two of stairs at a brisk, steady pace for about four minutes, breathing hard but still able to speak, then wait at the top until your breathing settles and your legs feel steady, and walk back down slowly, holding the rail. At home you hold a wall sit against a clear wall, away from any stairs, for up to a minute, then lie on a mat with knees bent and let the tremor run for up to 15 minutes, ending it whenever you like by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and stay still for two minutes before getting up. A provider teaches the sequence first and checks that your stair route is safe.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never exercise without a playlist, who want a stronger, more athletic version of shaking practice, and who have easy access to stairs.
modalities.cautions: It is an untested idea and genuinely tiring, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or balance problems, epilepsy or seizures, are pregnant, or have had recent surgery, fractures or injuries, warm up first, hold the handrail, and stop climbing for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Stop the tremor at any time by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, stop if you feel overwhelmed, spaced out or in pain, and people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider.
modalities.tweet: Prototype for people who never exercise without a playlist: Flights Without a Beat. Four brisk minutes on the stairs in silence, an easy walk down, a short wall sit at home, then lie down and let your tired legs tremble. Your breath sets the pace.
